resumen: A mechanical device that stops a suspended platform in the event of overspeed, excessive tilt or manual activation. I developed it in-house all the way to production, and it is now on sale.

bloques.intro: A suspended platform hangs from a working rope. A second rope, the safety rope, runs through the device and carries no load in normal use. If something fails, the device grips that rope and locks the platform.

pasos.texto: The platform moves up and down and the safety rope runs freely through the device. The jaws stay latched open and the device does not act.
The platform first descends at normal speed and then drops too fast. Above 0.5 m/s the rope spins the governor pulley faster than allowed, the mechanism trips and the jaws clamp onto the rope.

With two hoists, one end can rise faster than the other. What matters is the platform’s angle to the ground: above 14°, the safety rope, kept vertical by a counterweight, touches the trip lever and the device locks the platform.
While the platform is descending normally, pressing the emergency button stops it abruptly: the trip lever releases the jaws, which clamp the rope.

parrafos: The design went through about nine versions, five or six of them built as physical prototypes. I took the project through to the final product.

Every version followed the same loop: design, review with the project lead, drawings, parts order, inspection of incoming parts, assembly, feedback from workshop technicians, testing and conclusions. The technicians, who check bought-in fall arresters every day, pointed out the problems that show up in real use.

bloques.texto: The device can be mounted on hoist motors or other structures. It is built up between side plates and closed with covers.

tabla.v: On hoist motors or other structures
Overspeed (above 0.5 m/s), tilt (above 14°) or emergency button
Manual, with a lever, as many times as needed
Laser cutting, welding, machining, turning, waterjet cutting and sheet-metal bending

bloques.intro: Animated 2D diagrams of the three subsystems, in the order in which they act: the governor measures speed, the trip mechanism decides and the jaws grip the rope.

parrafos: The pressure arm presses the rope against the governor pulley, so the pulley turns in proportion to the platform’s vertical speed.
The governor is set to stay closed below the critical speed. When the platform descends faster than 0.5 m/s, the governor opens.
The handle resets the mechanism, which stays latched in the working position as long as there is no overspeed.
If the governor opens, the trip mechanism fires and frees the jaws that grip the rope. It is also designed so that, at a tilt above 14°, the rope touches the mechanism and trips it, freeing the jaws.
If the emergency button is pressed, it also trips the mechanism, which releases the jaws.
In the working position the jaws stay open and let the safety rope run freely. When the device trips, torsion springs close them onto the rope.
As an additional safety feature, they can only be reopened once the load is back on the working rope.

bloques.intro: Once the design was finished, this is what I did to take it into production and onto the market.

items.texto: I produced the final manufacturing and assembly drawings for every part and mechanism. Whenever a part changed, I issued a new drawing revision so that suppliers always worked to the current version.

I contacted suppliers and part manufacturers to get quotes for large production runs and to find the critical parts worth optimising. During prototyping I had already worked with three suppliers: machining and turning, laser cutting and welding, and waterjet cutting.

I designed and ran the tests required for certification to UNE-EN 1808:2016. With three V8 prototypes I carried out 15 drop tests at 500 kg: every arrest distance was between 6 and 9 cm, against the 50 cm the standard allows. In the tilt test on a real platform the device tripped between 11.8° and 12.7°, below the 14° limit in the standard. These were in-house tests, without external certification.
I coordinated the manufacture of 20 units, released in two batches of 10, and oversaw the start-up of the process.
I trained the technicians to assemble and maintain the devices. I prepared the assembly drawings, trained two workshop technicians and supervised the assembly of 10 units, with no design issues.

items.titulo: Bill of materials in the ERP
items.texto: I built the bill of materials for the device and each subassembly in the ERP to automate manufacturing orders, give every device a serial number, track part and product stock, and manage drawing revisions and design changes. Each part has its own item code, with supplier and price by order quantity, and when an order is released the system checks stock and alerts purchasing.

bloques.texto: The device is manufactured and sold. The company used to buy fall arresters from other manufacturers for its platforms. Now it assembles its own.
